PSYCHIATRIC__Low Mood:
Low mood is a symptom, and the first move is always to assess risk. Before anything else, ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans, intent and means — a positive answer changes the plan immediately (see self-harm & suicidal ideation). Then decide: is this clinical depression, and is it unipolar or bipolar? Core depression is persistent low mood, anhedonia and low energy for ≥2 weeks with cognitive and biological symptoms (see depressive disorders). Always ask about past mania / hypomania — bipolar depression must not be treated with antidepressant monotherapy (see bipolar disorder, mania). And exclude organic causes: hypothyroidism, anaemia / B12 deficiency, drugs (steroids, beta-blockers, alcohol), Cushing’s, Parkinson’s, dementia and occult malignancy (see hypothyroidism, anaemia, substance use). Don’t forget bereavement and adjustment, and comorbid anxiety.
🚨Assess suicide risk in everyone with low mood. Ask about ideation, plans, intent, means, and protective factors; escalate for a specific plan, intent, access to means, previous attempts, or command hallucinations (see self-harm & suicidal ideation, self-harm & suicide risk). Severe / psychotic depression — delusions of guilt, poverty or nihilism (Cotard’s), catatonia, or severe self-neglect and dehydration — is a psychiatric emergency needing urgent assessment (± ECT) (see depressive disorders). Screen for bipolarity (a past “high”) before prescribing (see bipolar disorder), and think of postnatal depression (and puerperal psychosis) in the perinatal period.

1Confirm & classify
🚩Suicide / self-harm risk
  • Ask directly: ideation, plan, intent, means, previous attempts, protective factors
  • Command hallucinations, hopelessness, impulsivity raise risk → risk assessment + safety plan (see self-harm & suicidal ideation, self-harm & suicide risk)
  • Consider urgent psychiatry / admission
🚩Psychotic / severe depression
  • Mood-congruent delusions (guilt, poverty, nihilism / Cotard’s), hallucinations
  • Catatonia, stupor, severe self-neglect / dehydration → urgent assessment ± ECT (see depressive disorders)
  • A psychiatric emergency
🟠Bipolar depression
  • A past episode of mania / hypomania (elevated mood, reduced need for sleep, overspending, grandiosity)
  • Antidepressant monotherapy can trigger a switch — screen before prescribing (see bipolar disorder, mania)
  • Needs a mood stabiliser-based plan
🟠Organic cause
  • Hypothyroidism, anaemia / B12 deficiency, Cushing’s, Parkinson’s, dementia, occult cancer (see hypothyroidism, anaemia)
  • Drugs / alcohol — steroids, beta-blockers, interferon, alcohol (see substance use)
  • Check TFTs, FBC, B12 / folate, glucose, calcium
🩹Unipolar depression
  • Low mood + anhedonia + low energy for ≥2 weeks
  • Plus sleep / appetite / concentration / guilt / worthlessness changes (see depressive disorders)
  • Grade severity (e.g. PHQ-9); the commonest cause
🩹Bereavement / adjustment
  • Grief — proportionate to a loss, comes in waves, preserved self-worth
  • Adjustment disorder after a stressor; seasonal affective disorder
  • Comorbid anxiety is common (see anxiety)
Risk, then bipolar, then organic. Always assess suicide risk; always ask about a past high (bipolar) before prescribing an antidepressant; and always exclude organic causes (thyroid, anaemia, drugs / alcohol) of low mood.

3Assess & act
At the bedside — the risk, the mental state, the past “high”, the organic screen
History & red flags
Core symptoms (mood, anhedonia, energy) + duration; biological (sleep, appetite, weight, libido) and cognitive (guilt, worthlessness, concentration) features; suicidal ideation / plan; past mania; alcohol / drugs; thyroid / anaemia symptoms; perinatal; recent loss / stressor
Examine
A focused mental state examination — appearance / behaviour, speech, mood and affect, thought content (guilt / nihilism / suicidal), perception (hallucinations), cognition and insight; look for psychomotor retardation, self-neglect, and physical signs of an organic cause (thyroid, pallor)
Investigate
Screen for organic causes: TFTs, FBC, B12 / folate, U&E, calcium, glucose / HbA1c, LFTs (± drug review); use a validated tool (PHQ-9); a formal risk assessment; collateral history for bipolarity
Act
Manage risk first (safety plan ± urgent psychiatry / admission); for depression, offer psychological therapy (and an antidepressant for moderate–severe), treating bipolar depression with a mood-stabiliser-based plan (not antidepressant monotherapy); treat the organic cause; and support bereavement / adjustment

Suicide risk → risk assessmentPsychotic depression → mental state exam (urgent psychiatry)Bipolar depression → collateral history of maniaOrganic cause → TFTs / FBC / B12 / calciumUnipolar depression → clinical (PHQ-9)Bereavement → clinical
The rules that carry it: assess suicide risk in everyone; screen for bipolarity before prescribing; exclude organic causes. Treat depression with therapy ± an antidepressant, and manage bipolar depression differently.

PSYCHIATRIC__Anxiety:
Anxiety is excessive fear or worry with autonomic arousal — palpitations, sweating, tremor, chest tightness, breathlessness and a sense of dread. The essential first step is to exclude the physical “masqueraders”, because several dangerous conditions present exactly like a panic attack: acute coronary syndrome, an arrhythmia, pulmonary embolism, hypoglycaemia and thyroid storm (see acute coronary syndrome). Then screen for endocrine and drug causes — hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, caffeine / stimulants and alcohol / benzodiazepine withdrawal (see hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, substance use). Only then classify the primary anxiety disorder: generalised anxiety disorder (persistent free-floating worry), panic disorder (recurrent unexpected panic attacks), phobias (specific, social, agoraphobia) and health anxiety (see anxiety & stress-related disorders). Anxiety very commonly coexists with depression, PTSD and OCD (see low mood, PTSD, OCD).
🚨Do not label a first “panic attack” without excluding a physical emergency. Chest pain with cardiac risk factors needs an ECG and troponin to exclude acute coronary syndrome or an arrhythmia (see acute coronary syndrome); sudden breathlessness with risk factors needs a PE work-up; and always check a capillary glucose (hypoglycaemia). Endocrine mimics are treatable: hyperthyroidism (weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance, tachycardia) and phaeochromocytoma (paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating) (see hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma). Consider substance / withdrawal states (see substance use), and screen for comorbid depression and suicide risk (see low mood).

🚩Physical emergency mimic
  • Panic-like presentation from ACS / arrhythmia, PE, hypoglycaemia, thyroid storm
  • → ECG + troponin, PE work-up, capillary glucose as indicated (see acute coronary syndrome)
  • Especially a first episode, older age, cardiac risk factors
🚩Endocrine cause
  • Hyperthyroidism — weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance, tachycardia (see hyperthyroidism)
  • Phaeochromocytoma — paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating, palpitations (see phaeochromocytoma)
  • Check TFTs; metanephrines if paroxysmal + hypertensive
🟠Panic disorder
  • Recurrent unexpected panic attacks (peak ~10 min) + anticipatory fear
  • Fear of dying / losing control, catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations (see anxiety disorders)
  • May develop agoraphobia
🟠Generalised anxiety disorder
  • Persistent, free-floating worry most days for ≥6 months
  • Restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance (see anxiety disorders)
  • Grade with GAD-7
🩹Phobias / social anxiety
  • Specific phobia (situation / object), social anxiety (fear of scrutiny), agoraphobia
  • Marked avoidance and anticipatory anxiety (see anxiety disorders)
  • Cued, predictable anxiety
🩹Comorbid / substance
  • Depression (very common overlap), PTSD, OCD (see low mood, PTSD, OCD)
  • Caffeine / stimulants, alcohol / benzodiazepine withdrawal (see substance use)
  • Treat the driver, not just the symptom
Exclude the body first. A panic attack and an MI, PE, hypoglycaemia or thyroid storm feel the same to the patient. Rule out the physical and endocrine causes, then classify the anxiety disorder and screen for comorbid depression and substances.

PSYCHIATRIC__Psychosis:
Psychosis is a loss of contact with reality — hallucinations, delusions, thought disorder and loss of insight. The golden rule is that a first episode of psychosis is organic until proven otherwise. Before reaching for a psychiatric label, exclude delirium (an acute, fluctuating, clouded consciousness with disorientation and, classically, visual hallucinations — find and treat the cause) (see delirium, confusion / delirium), drugs and withdrawal (stimulants, cannabis, hallucinogens, steroids; alcohol withdrawal / delirium tremens) (see substance use), and medical / neurological causes (autoimmune encephalitis, temporal-lobe epilepsy, Lewy body dementia). Only then classify the functional psychoses: schizophrenia (see schizophrenia / psychosis), mood psychoses (psychotic depression and mania) (see low mood, mania), schizoaffective and delusional disorder. Puerperal psychosis is a postpartum emergency (see postpartum complications).
🚨Screen every first-episode psychosis for an organic cause. Delirium (clouded / fluctuating consciousness) demands a search for infection, metabolic disturbance, drugs and CNS disease (see delirium). Autoimmune (anti-NMDA-receptor) encephalitis — psychosis with confusion, seizures, movement disorder and autonomic instability in a young person — is treatable and must not be missed (see encephalitis). Puerperal psychosis (rapid-onset postpartum psychosis / confusion) is a psychiatric emergency (see postpartum complications). Assess risk throughout — command hallucinations, delusion-driven acts, suicide and neglect — and remember drug-induced psychosis (stimulants, cannabis) (see substance use).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Delirium (organic psychosis)
  • Acute onset, fluctuating course, clouded consciousness, disorientation, inattention
  • Classically visual hallucinations → find and treat the cause (infection, metabolic, drugs, CNS) (see delirium, confusion / delirium)
  • Not schizophrenia — the level of consciousness is impaired
🚩Encephalitis / CNS cause
  • Autoimmune (anti-NMDA) or infective encephalitis — psychosis + confusion, seizures, movement disorder, autonomic instability
  • Temporal-lobe epilepsy, tumour, Lewy body dementia (see encephalitis)
  • LP + MRI + antibodies; treatable
🚩Puerperal psychosis / risk
  • Rapid-onset postpartum psychosis / confusion — a psychiatric emergency (see postpartum complications)
  • Command hallucinations, delusion-driven acts, suicide / harm to others or infant
  • Assess and manage risk urgently
🟠Drug-induced / withdrawal
  • Stimulants, cannabis, hallucinogens, steroids; alcohol withdrawal / delirium tremens (see substance use)
  • Onset relates to use / cessation; often resolves
  • Urine drug screen; treat withdrawal
🟠Schizophrenia / functional
  • ≥1 month of delusions, auditory hallucinations (third-person / running commentary), thought disorder, passivity
  • Negative symptoms (blunted affect, avolition, social withdrawal), preserved consciousness (see schizophrenia / psychosis)
  • Schizoaffective / delusional disorder are relatives
🩹Mood psychosis
  • Psychotic depression — nihilistic / guilt delusions (see low mood)
  • Mania with grandiose delusions and pressured speech (see mania)
  • Mood-congruent psychosis; treat the mood disorder
Consciousness is the great divider. Clouded / fluctuating consciousness = delirium (organic — find the cause). Clear consciousness with delusions / hallucinations for ≥1 month points to a functional psychosis — but still screen for drugs and encephalitis.

Visual vs auditory. Visual hallucinations with clouded consciousness suggest an organic cause (delirium, drugs, Lewy body); auditory hallucinations (voices) in clear consciousness suggest a functional psychosis. Mood symptoms reframe it as a mood psychosis.

At the bedside — the level of consciousness, the mental state, the drug history, the risk
History & red flags
Onset and course (acute / fluctuating vs insidious), level of consciousness; drugs / alcohol; mood symptoms; postpartum; seizures / neurological symptoms; risk (command hallucinations, delusion-driven acts, suicide, neglect); collateral history and duration
Examine
A full mental state examination (appearance, speech, mood, thought form / content, perception, cognition, insight) plus a physical and neurological examination; assess orientation and attention (delirium), pyrexia, and drug-withdrawal signs
Investigate
Organic screen: FBC, U&E, LFTs, glucose, calcium, TFTs, CRP, cultures, urine drug screen, and (as indicated) CT / MRI brain, LP and autoimmune / infective encephalitis antibodies; use collateral to establish duration and course
Act
Treat the organic cause (infection, drugs, encephalitis, delirium); for a functional psychosis, refer to early-intervention psychiatry and start an antipsychotic; manage the mood disorder in mood psychosis; treat puerperal psychosis urgently (mother-and-baby unit); manage risk throughout

PSYCHIATRIC__Mania:
Mania is elevated or irritable mood with increased energy and activity. The symptom cluster is DIGFAST — Distractibility, Insomnia (reduced need for sleep), Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, increased Activity, pressured Speech and Thoughtless risk-taking (spending, sex, driving). Mania lasts ≥1 week with marked impairment (± psychosis); hypomania lasts ≥4 days without severe impairment or psychosis (see bipolar disorder). As with any first presentation, exclude secondary causes: drugs (steroids, dopamine agonists, stimulants, an antidepressant-induced switch) (see drug reactions, substance use), hyperthyroidism (see hyperthyroidism), and frontal-lobe pathology or delirium. Assess risk throughout — financial, sexual, physical exhaustion, and psychosis (see psychosis, self-harm & suicidal ideation).
🚨Acute mania is a psychiatric emergency of risk. Manic patients can bankrupt themselves, drive dangerously, become sexually disinhibited, and reach physical exhaustion and dehydration; grandiose or persecutory psychosis may drive dangerous acts (see psychosis). Screen for secondary mania — corticosteroids, dopamine agonists, stimulants and an antidepressant-induced switch (see drug reactions), and hyperthyroidism (see hyperthyroidism). Do not forget that mania is one pole of bipolar disorder — an antidepressant given for the depressive phase can trigger a switch, and lithium / valproate have their own toxicity and (valproate) teratogenicity (see bipolar disorder).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Severe mania with psychosis / risk
  • Grandiose / persecutory delusions, reckless spending / sex / driving, aggression
  • Physical exhaustion, dehydration, self-neglect → urgent psychiatry ± admission (see bipolar disorder, psychosis)
  • Assess risk to self, others and finances
🚩Secondary (organic) mania
  • Corticosteroids, dopamine agonists, hyperthyroidism (see drug reactions, hyperthyroidism)
  • Frontal-lobe lesion / stroke, delirium, HIV / CNS disease
  • Screen with a drug review + TFTs; treat the cause
🟠Substance-induced
  • Stimulants (amphetamines, cocaine), antidepressant-induced switch (see substance use)
  • Onset relates to use; often settles on withdrawal
  • Urine drug screen; review the drug chart
🟠Bipolar I — mania
  • ≥1 week of elevated / irritable mood + DIGFAST, marked impairment (± psychosis)
  • Alternates with depressive episodes (see bipolar disorder, low mood)
  • Mood stabiliser (lithium / valproate) ± antipsychotic
🩹Hypomania (bipolar II)
  • ≥4 days of elevated mood + increased activity, no marked impairment or psychosis
  • With recurrent depressive episodes = bipolar II (see bipolar disorder)
  • Often under-recognised; ask about past highs
🩹Other / differential
  • Cyclothymia (chronic mild mood instability)
  • ADHD, personality traits, agitated / mixed depression
  • Mixed states carry a high suicide risk
Duration and impairment. ≥1 week + marked impairment (± psychosis) = mania; ≥4 days without severe impairment = hypomania. Always exclude secondary causes (drugs, steroids, thyroid) and assess risk.

Reduced need for sleep is the giveaway. The manic patient feels rested after little sleep, unlike the exhausted insomniac. And a new drug or hyperthyroidism can produce the whole picture — screen before labelling it bipolar.
3Assess & act
At the bedside — the DIGFAST picture, the duration, the drugs / thyroid, the risk
History & red flags
Duration (≥1 week vs ≥4 days), DIGFAST symptoms, reduced need for sleep; risk behaviours (spending, sex, driving); drugs / steroids / stimulants / antidepressants; thyroid symptoms; past depressive / manic episodes; psychosis; collateral history
Examine
Mental state examination — overactivity, elevated / irritable affect, pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose delusions, distractibility, impaired judgement and insight; physical exam for thyroid signs and exhaustion / dehydration
Investigate
A drug / substance review, urine drug screen, TFTs, U&E and glucose; baseline bloods before starting a mood stabiliser (renal / thyroid function, pregnancy test); collateral history to establish the pattern
Act
Ensure safety (± admission, Mental Health Act if needed); stop an antidepressant / culprit drug; start an antipsychotic for acute mania and a mood stabiliser (lithium or valproate — not valproate in women of childbearing potential) for maintenance; treat the secondary cause; manage risk and hydration
Then — confirm the cause
Severe mania → urgent psychiatrySecondary mania → drug review + TFTsSubstance-induced → urine drug screenBipolar I mania → clinical (≥1 week + impairment)Hypomania → clinical (≥4 days)Mixed state → risk assessment
The rules that carry it: ≥1 week + impairment = mania, ≥4 days = hypomania. Exclude secondary causes (drugs / steroids / thyroid). Stop antidepressants, use an antipsychotic + mood stabiliser, and manage risk.

PSYCHIATRIC__Memory Loss:
The first question in memory loss is: acute or chronic? Acute memory impairment is usually delirium (an organic, fluctuating, inattentive confusional state — find the cause) (see delirium, confusion / delirium), or a discrete event — Wernicke’s encephalopathy, transient global amnesia, head injury or seizure (see Wernicke-Korsakoff, transient global amnesia). Chronic, progressive memory loss suggests dementia (Alzheimer’s, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal) (see dementias). The crucial task is to catch the reversible “dementia mimics”: depression (pseudodementia) (see depressive disorders, low mood), hypothyroidism, B12 / folate deficiency (see hypothyroidism, anaemia), normal-pressure hydrocephalus (dementia + gait apraxia + incontinence) (see hydrocephalus), and medications / alcohol. Always take a collateral history.
🚨Some memory loss is a treatable emergency. Wernicke’s encephalopathy — the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia / nystagmus and ataxia, classically in an alcohol-dependent or malnourished patient — needs immediate parenteral thiamine to prevent irreversible Korsakoff’s amnesia (give thiamine before glucose) (see Wernicke-Korsakoff). Acute memory loss is often delirium — screen for infection, drugs and metabolic causes (see delirium). Normal-pressure hydrocephalus (the triad of dementia, a magnetic gait and urinary incontinence) is reversible with shunting (see hydrocephalus). And depression can masquerade as dementia (pseudodementia) — and is treatable (see depressive disorders).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Delirium (acute organic)
  • Acute onset, fluctuating course, inattention, clouded consciousness
  • Infection, drugs, metabolic, retention / constipation, hypoxia → find and treat the cause (see delirium, confusion / delirium)
  • Superimposed on dementia is common
🚩Wernicke’s encephalopathy
  • Triad of confusion + ophthalmoplegia / nystagmus + ataxia (alcohol / malnutrition)
  • → immediate parenteral thiamine (before glucose) to prevent Korsakoff’s amnesia (see Wernicke-Korsakoff)
  • Korsakoff’s = amnesia + confabulation
🟠Reversible dementia mimics
  • Depression (pseudodementia), hypothyroidism, B12 / folate deficiency (see depressive disorders, hypothyroidism, anaemia)
  • Normal-pressure hydrocephalus (dementia + gait + incontinence, reversible) (see hydrocephalus)
  • Drugs (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines), alcohol
🟠Dementia (chronic progressive)
  • Alzheimer’s (insidious, amnestic), vascular (stepwise, vascular risk), Lewy body (fluctuation, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism), frontotemporal (behaviour / language) (see dementias)
  • Impairs daily function; clear consciousness
  • Cognitive testing + imaging + reversible screen
🩹Transient global amnesia
  • Sudden isolated anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning
  • Resolves within 24 hours, no other neurology, self-limiting (see transient global amnesia)
  • Exclude seizure / TIA (transient epileptic amnesia)
🩹MCI / normal ageing / functional
  • Mild cognitive impairment — measurable deficit, function preserved
  • Benign age-related forgetfulness; anxiety / functional memory complaints
  • Monitor; a proportion of MCI progresses to dementia
Acute vs chronic, and always screen for reversibility. Acute → delirium / Wernicke’s / TGA. Chronic progressive → dementia — but first exclude depression, thyroid, B12 and NPH. Collateral history is essential.

PSYCHIATRIC__Sleep Disturbance:
Sleep disturbance is a symptom to explain, not a diagnosis. Sort it into insomnia (difficulty falling / staying asleep), hypersomnia (excessive daytime sleepiness), circadian problems (shift work, jet lag, delayed sleep phase) and parasomnias (sleepwalking, terrors, REM sleep behaviour disorder, nightmares). Most insomnia is secondary — to depression (early-morning waking), anxiety (a racing mind at sleep onset), pain, caffeine, alcohol and drugs (see low mood, anxiety). The most important medical cause of unrefreshing sleep is obstructive sleep apnoea — loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas and daytime somnolence, with real cardiovascular risk (see obstructive sleep apnoea, snoring & apnoeas). And don’t miss the psychiatric flags: a reduced need for sleep in mania and insomnia with suicidal depression (see mania). Consider restless legs, narcolepsy and REM sleep behaviour disorder (see restless legs, sleep disorders).
🚨Sleep symptoms can flag serious disease. Obstructive sleep apnoea (snoring + witnessed apnoeas + daytime somnolence, often with obesity and hypertension) raises the risk of road-traffic accidents, hypertension, arrhythmia and stroke — it needs a sleep study and CPAP (see obstructive sleep apnoea). A markedly reduced need for sleep with elevated mood is mania (see mania); insomnia with pervasive low mood should prompt a suicide-risk assessment (see low mood). REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams, punching / shouting) can herald Parkinson’s disease / Lewy body dementia years ahead (see Parkinson’s disease). And avoid the trap of long-term hypnotics / benzodiazepines.

🚩Obstructive sleep apnoea
  • Loud snoring + witnessed apnoeas + daytime somnolence, unrefreshing sleep
  • Obesity, large neck, hypertension → road-traffic / cardiovascular risk; sleep study + CPAP (see obstructive sleep apnoea, snoring & apnoeas)
  • The key treatable cause of hypersomnolence
🚩Psychiatric emergency
  • Reduced need for sleep + elevated mood / overactivity = mania (see mania)
  • Insomnia with pervasive low mood → assess suicide risk (see low mood)
  • Sleep change is a core mood-disorder symptom
🟠Secondary insomnia
  • Depression (early-morning waking), anxiety (racing mind at onset), pain (see low mood, anxiety)
  • Caffeine, alcohol, nicotine, stimulants, steroids; withdrawal states
  • Treat the cause + sleep hygiene / CBT-I
🟠Restless legs / narcolepsy
  • Restless legs — urge to move the legs at night, relieved by movement (check ferritin) (see restless legs)
  • Narcolepsy — excessive daytime sleepiness + cataplexy + sleep paralysis + hypnagogic hallucinations (see sleep disorders)
  • Periodic limb movement disorder
🩹Circadian rhythm disorder
  • Shift work, jet lag, delayed sleep-phase (teenagers)
  • Sleep is normal but mistimed (see sleep disorders)
  • Light therapy, timed melatonin, schedule change
🩹Parasomnias
  • Sleepwalking, night terrors (non-REM, children)
  • REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams) — a marker of Parkinson’s / Lewy body (see Parkinson’s disease)
  • Nightmares and hyperarousal in PTSD (see PTSD)
Insomnia is usually secondary. Hunt the cause — depression, anxiety, pain, drugs, caffeine, alcohol. For daytime sleepiness, think OSA first. And read the sleep symptom as a possible mood-disorder flag.

PSYCHIATRIC__Eating & Appetite Changes:
Read eating and appetite changes on two axes: weight direction and appetite direction. Weight loss with a poor appetite raises depression, malignancy and chronic disease; weight loss with a preserved / increased appetite points to hyperthyroidism or new type 1 diabetes (see hyperthyroidism, type 1 diabetes). Weight gain follows hypothyroidism, Cushing’s, PCOS and drugs (antipsychotics, steroids) or atypical depression (see hypothyroidism, Cushing’s, PCOS, weight gain). Then screen for the eating disorders: anorexia nervosa (restriction, low BMI, intense fear of weight gain), bulimia (binge–purge, usually normal weight), binge-eating disorder and ARFID (see eating disorders). Two things are medical emergencies: the medically unstable anorexic (bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, electrolyte disturbance, refeeding risk) and purging hypokalaemia (arrhythmia). Ask the SCOFF questions.
🚨The starved and the purging body can arrest. In anorexia nervosa, watch for medical instability — a very low BMI, bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, prolonged QTc and electrolyte disturbance — and for refeeding syndrome (falling phosphate / potassium / magnesium on feeding) which can be fatal (see eating disorders). Purging in bulimia causes hypokalaemia and arrhythmia, a metabolic alkalosis and Russell’s sign (knuckle callus). Do not miss organic weight loss: malignancy (unintentional loss + red flags), hyperthyroidism, and new type 1 diabetes presenting with weight loss, polyuria and thirst — which can proceed to DKA (see hyperthyroidism, type 1 diabetes).

  • New type 1 diabetes (weight loss + polyuria + thirst → DKA) (see type 1 diabetes)

  • Recurrent binge–purge, usually normal weight, shape / weight over-concern

  • Check U&E; ECG if symptomatic

  • Reduced appetite + weight loss (or atypical increased appetite / weight) (see low mood)
  • Anhedonia, low mood, biological symptoms; assess suicide risk
  • A common, treatable cause of appetite change

  • Hypothyroidism, Cushing’s syndrome, PCOS (see hypothyroidism, Cushing’s, PCOS)
  • Drugs — antipsychotics, steroids, sodium valproate, insulin (see weight gain)

  • Body-image distortion (except ARFID); amenorrhoea; laxative / exercise misuse
  • Screen with SCOFF; multidisciplinary care
